transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Liam (Head of ML - Bluecrest), Priya (CTO), Marcus (Quant Engineer)

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um quick intro - I'm Sofia, AE at Redwood, and with me is Ethan our SE.
[00:08] Ethan: Hi all, happy to walk through cost and performance tradeoffs and dig into their workload.
[00:13] Liam: Thanks, Sofia. We're excited - Bluecrest runs a couple workloads: short chat assist and heavy reranking for candidate lists, so both latency and per-token costs matter.
[00:25] Priya: timeline is Q2 pilot, Q3 decision ideally. Budget is tight; we need clear unit economics.
[00:33] Sofia: Great, that's helpful. Quick qualification: where are you running models today? cloud or self-hosted?
[00:38] Marcus: Mostly self-hosted on EC2 + mixed GPUs, plus some API usage with OpenAI for experiments. We want to avoid runaway costs and keep IP on-prem for some pipelines.
[00:49] Ethan: Cool. To frame the convo: we'll cover hosted API pricing, dedicated reserved pools, and private deployments; then dive into batching/caching levers that materially change per-token cost.
[01:02] Liam: Perfect. Can you quantify the effect of batching and prefix/KV cache - like what I should expect for our reranking job?
[01:09] Ethan: Absolutely. Roughly speaking, batching increases throughput and reduces per-token GPU overhead but adds queuing latency. For short sequences typical in rerank, you can batch a lot - if you can tolerate a 10-30ms added scheduling delay you may cut per-token cost 20-60% depending on model and GPU.
[01:30] Priya: And KV/prefix cache? We have lots of repeated context in our pricing models, maybe 30-40% reuse on prefixes.
[01:38] Ethan: If you have a high prefix-hit rate, KV cache is huge. For autoregressive generation, a cache hit means you skip re-computing past keys and only compute incremental tokens - that can reduce compute ~30-70% depending on sequence distribution. So those two together - batching + cache - stack.
[01:56] Marcus: Are those behaviors available on Hosted immediately or do we need Dedicated?
[02:01] Ethan: Hosted supports intelligent batching and caching at the platform level, yes. The difference is control: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and deterministic throughput, and you can tune batching windows more aggressively without noisy neighbors. Hosted has strong defaults and auto-burst but if predictable p50/p95 is required, Dedicated is recommended.
[02:20] Liam: For our quick rerank pipeline, target p50 < 200ms and p95 < 500ms. Is that feasible on Hosted or only Dedicated?
[02:29] Ethan: It depends on throughput. For small models and low concurrency, Hosted can hit that. As rps grows and if you need strict SLOs, Dedicated's reserved capacity reduces variance. We typically see Hosted p50 ~120-220ms for short prompts on our curated medium models under moderate load; Dedicated can bring p95 down by removing cross-tenant jitter.
[02:48] Priya: Can you break out pricing - per-token vs instance-level? We're trying to compare a per-token hosted plan versus committing to dedicated GPUs monthly.
[02:58] Sofia: Sure, high level: Hosted is per-token and scales linearly with usage - good for experimentation and variable workloads. Dedicated is a reserved monthly cost for pools; unit cost becomes a function of utilization. If you commit and hit high utilization, cost/token can be significantly lower than hosted. Private installs have a license/infra cost plus ops overhead. We'll send a spreadsheet with example TCO.
[03:16] Liam: Any numbers to ballpark right now? even relative multipliers help.
[03:20] Ethan: Ballpark, for inference-optimized medium models: Hosted might be X per 1k tokens; Dedicated, assuming 60-80% utilization, could be 0.4-0.7X per 1k tokens - big variance depends on batching and KV hit rates. Also quantization and model selection matter: int8/4 quantized variants can reduce GPU footprint further.
[03:40] Marcus: About quantization: do you support mixed-precision or int8 inference? how's the quality hit?
[03:45] Ethan: We support quantized runtimes and maintain quality by validating on your eval sets. For many open models, int8 or Q4_0 shows minimal quality degradation for classification/reranking; for sensitive generation prompts we recommend validating. Our Optimize tooling recommends quantization profiles per workload.
[04:01] Priya: If we run private deployment for IP reasons, do we still get caching/batching benefits?
[04:06] Ethan: Yes. The serving runtime is the same; caching and batching are part of the engine. With Private, you run the runtime in your VPC or on-prem; you get control but manage infra, and we provide the control plane integration if desired.
[04:20] Liam: Security checklist - SOC2, SSO, KMS. We need to know hosted encryption at rest and key management.
[04:27] Sofia: We will share the SOC2 pack. Hosted supports customer-managed keys via KMS for dedicated/private tiers; audit logs and RBAC are available. Private gives you full key control. We'll attach the security doc to the follow-up.
[04:40] Marcus: For benchmarking, what telemetry do you recommend we capture?
[04:44] Ethan: p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, batch sizes, cache hit rates, and memory/3rd party logs. We'll send a benchmark checklist with sample prompts and seq length distributions.
[04:54] Priya: About burst handling - sometimes we have sudden spikes in scoring. Can Dedicated burst into hosted or a higher tier?
[05:02] Ethan: Yes, we have smart routing and fallback policies - with Dedicated you can configure burst capacity into hosted or a warm pool. Smart routing can also fallback to cheaper model variants if capacity constrained.
[05:15] Liam: Competitors - any differences vs Lambda Labs or Anthropic in how you price?
[05:21] Sofia: The main difference is our focus on production cost controls and observability. Some vendors have straightforward per-instance pricing; ours couples runtime optimizations and tooling (batching, cache, quantization recommendations) into TCO models and dashboards.
[05:33] Priya: On the hosted per-token pricing, what's included - do we charge for tokens consumed during caching or just generated tokens?
[05:40] Ethan: Per-token billing counts model compute tokens processed by the runtime. If KV/prefix cache avoids recomputation of tokens, those avoided tokens aren't billed. There's nuance for certain features (e.g., structured tool calls) - we'll include specifics in the pricing sheet.
[05:56] Marcus: For reranking, we often run many short queries in parallel - does Redwood support micro-batching efficiently or is there overhead?
[06:04] Ethan: Micro-batching is supported. The runtime uses continuous batching; overhead is minimal. Tuning batch windows and priority scheduling helps keep latencies low while getting batching gains.
[06:15] Liam: Let's talk scenario numbers - say 2M tokens/day, 200 qps during peak, average seq length 8 tokens, 40% cache hit rate. What model of cost do we run? Hosted would be pretty expensive maybe?
[06:28] Ethan: We'd run back-of-envelope in the TCO sheet, but qualitatively: with heavy batching and 40% cache hit rate, per-token compute decreases a lot. If you expect consistent steady-state usage, Dedicated with 24/7 reserved capacity gives best unit cost; Hosted is simpler for variability. We'll run exact numbers in the spreadsheet.
[06:45] Priya: On contract terms for Dedicated, can we do monthly commitments first? we prefer not to lock a year.
[06:51] Sofia: Yes, we offer monthly and annual reserved tiers. Monthly has less discount but more flexibility.
[06:58] Liam: For the pilot, what metrics will decide success?
[07:02] Marcus: p50 < 200ms for rerank, cost per 1k tokens under X (we'll give a target in the next day), and demonstration of cache hit >=30%.
[07:12] Ethan: Good. We'll also track model quality regression on your eval set as a hard stop. Redwood Optimize can monitor regressions.
[07:20] Priya: Any hidden costs we should be worried about - egress, logs, storage?
[07:25] Sofia: Egress in hosted is standard cloud egress; logs and retention are configurable and may be add-ons for long-term retention. We'll detail that.
[07:33] Liam: Operationally, who runs the private deployment ops? our infra team or Redwood?
[07:38] Ethan: We offer options - you can self-manage with our on-prem package and docs, or we can provide a managed private setup as an add-on. That affects costs.
[07:47] Priya: Sounds good. On latency, if we move to quantized smaller models to save cost, what's the latency tradeoff?
[07:54] Ethan: Smaller/quantized models can reduce compute and often improve latency; but depends on kernels and CPU/GPU characteristics. Quantization sometimes improves throughput on certain kernels. We'll validate on your workload.
[08:06] Marcus: For the demo/pilot, we'll want a canary rollout plan and rollback if we see quality drop.
[08:12] Ethan: That's built into our rollout features - canary percentages, fallback to previous model variant, and automatic A/B comparisons.
[08:20] Sofia: Recap - we'll send pricing TCO sheet with hosted vs dedicated vs private scenarios, security pack, benchmarking prompts and checklist, and propose a 2-hour demo for Marcus and infra next week.
[08:32] Liam: Thanks, that sounds perfect.
[08:35] Priya: Any other questions from you two?
[08:38] Marcus: none from me.
[08:40] Ethan: quick note - for the benchmarking guide we'll include suggested batch window params to replicate our observed savings.
[08:46] Sofia: Great. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the materials.

(Transcript continues with short Q&A and brief cross-talk at the end; the recording is truncated for brevity in export)

Final recap (automated): Next steps: pricing sheet, benchmark checklist, schedule demo. Action items recorded.
